Laboratory studies of Brazilian clam shrimp (Cyclestheria hislopi) reveal that neonates emerge from resting eggs with a carapace length of just 0.1 cm [Lb = 0.1 cm], a diminutive size that underscores their reliance on rapid early growth to escape gape-limited predation in ephemeral pools. After approximately 66 days [am = approximately 66 days] when reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], individuals typically reach the end of their natural lifespan, a duration that places them among the shorter-lived branchiopods. This comparatively compressed life cycle is an adaptive response to the unpredictable hydroperiods of their temporary aquatic habitats, where desiccation risk imposes strong selection for rapid completion of the reproductive phase before the habitat dries. Growth during the juvenile stage is notably efficient, allowing a newly hatched individual to increase its body size approximately threefold from the initial carapace length over the course of development. The carapace dimensions themselves are modest throughout life, never exceeding the maximum recorded length observed in fully mature specimens, a pattern that reflects the constraints of life in small, nutrient-limited water bodies.

Fully grown adults of Cyclestheria hislopi attain a maximum carapace length of 0.3 cm [Li = 0.3 cm], a size that corresponds to a terminal wet body mass of 0.0092 grams [Wwi = 0.0092 grams] in gravid females. These ultimate body dimensions are comparable to those reported for other small-bodied spinicaudatan clam shrimp inhabiting Neotropical temporary waters. The mass–length relationship underlying this value was derived from geometric approximation using measured carapace dimensions, confirming the allometric consistency of growth in this species. In contrast to the tiny hatchlings, which weigh an order of magnitude less, adults achieve a relatively robust body plan suitable for brooding successive clutches within the carapace chamber. The relatively modest size at full maturity reflects the energetic constraints of a microcrustacean exploiting a seasonally limited resource base in warm, shallow pools. This combination of small maximum body size and short lifespan defines the species as a classic r-selected strategist within the freshwater zooplankton community, prioritizing rapid population turnover over competitive dominance in stable habitats.

Puberty in Cyclestheria hislopi is attained when the carapace measures approximately 0.207 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.207 centimeters], marking the onset of functional reproductive capacity in young females. Reared at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], individuals achieve this developmental milestone roughly 15 days after birth [tp = roughly 15 days after birth], a remarkably brief period that allows the species to begin reproduction within the same hydroperiod in which it hatched. This rapid maturation is essential for population persistence in temporary pools where the aquatic phase may last only a few weeks. The carapace length at puberty is notably less than half the ultimate adult length, indicating that significant post-maturational growth continues even after females begin producing broods. This pattern of early puberty combined with continued somatic expansion is common among short-lived branchiopods that must balance the competing demands of current reproduction and future growth. The small size at first brood, typically around 0.27 centimeters, is consistent with the pattern observed in other clam shrimp genera such as Eocyzicus and Limnadia.

Female Cyclestheria hislopi produce multiple broods during their reproductive lifespan at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], with individual females typically depositing approximately 3.6 eggs at 22 days, 3.9 eggs at 30 days, and 3.9 eggs [N_R_i = 3.9 eggs] at 58 days, the latter value representing the maximum fecundity per clutch in this species. The reproductive strategy involves three distinct broods per year [F_R_i = three distinct broods per year] over the adult lifespan, each separated by an interbrood interval that lengthens as females age. These brood sizes are modest compared to those of larger conchostracans, but the repeated production of multiple clutches offsets the cost of small clutch size by extending the total reproductive output across the adult phase. Females carry the developing eggs within the carapace chamber, offering the progeny some protection from predation during early embryogenesis. The maximum daily reproductive output, calculated under these rearing conditions, reflects the 20 °C [T = 20 °C] thermal regime that approximates the species’ natural habitat temperature during the wet season. This rhythmic production of sequential broods maximizes the number of offspring released into the unpredictable pool environment before desiccation forces the termination of the aquatic phase.

Field-collected populations of Cyclestheria hislopi show considerable variability in the timing of sexual maturation, with the first brood typically occurring at 22 days [tR = at 22 days] under natural thermal conditions, a value that contrasts with the earlier pubertal timing observed under constant laboratory temperatures. The carapace length at this first reproductive event is approximately 0.27 centimeters [Lp = approximately 0.27 centimeters], notably larger than the 0.207 centimeters [Lp = 0.207 centimeters] recorded for the initial attainment of gonadal maturity, indicating a delay between physiological puberty and the first successful oviposition in the brood chamber. This lag likely reflects the time required for yolk accumulation and oocyte maturation following the activation of the reproductive system. The species’ life span, when determined under controlled laboratory conditions at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], averages 66 days [am = 66 days], with a range spanning 52 to 77 days depending on individual nutritional history and population density. This longevity estimate, while broadly consistent with that observed in other short-lived branchiopods, highlights the sensitivity of lifespan to thermal and nutritional conditions in temporary aquatic habitats, making Cyclestheria hislopi a valuable model for testing hypotheses about the ecological correlates of lifespan variation.
